title: Meta ships Muse Ember as the execution-layer model for agent workflows
subtitle: At $0.10 input and $0.50 output per million tokens, Ember is priced to run the repetitive subtasks that dominate an agent's token budget.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Meta released Muse Ember on November 9, 2026, the smallest and most efficient model in its Muse family. It is available through the Meta Model API and in Muse Code under the model ID muse-ember-1.0, priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens, and $0.50 per million output tokens. Context window is reportedly 1 million tokens with outputs up to 512K. Launch partners include Box, Cline, Oracle, Cloudflare, and You.com. Weights remain private, as with earlier Muse models.

Ember targets the execution layer of agent workflows — the high-volume, repetitive steps that dominate an agent's token spend: tool calls, routing decisions, document extraction, small coding subtasks. On Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, it scored 36, within one point of Claude Haiku 5.5 at a lower cost per task (roughly $0.14 versus $0.41 on the Artificial Analysis cost estimator). Meta positions larger Muse Wonder as the planner and Ember as the executor, an architectural split that mirrors the distinction Anthropic and OpenAI have been pushing in their agent documentation.

The broader context is that agent economics are becoming the dominant model-selection constraint. A frontier model at $8 input per million tokens is fine for the one planning step; it is prohibitive when the agent has to make 400 tool calls to finish a task. 2026 has produced a steady stream of cheap, specialized executor models — OpenAI's GPT-6 Nano, Anthropic's Haiku 5.5, now Meta's Muse Ember — all priced in the same range. For teams building agents at scale, choosing the right tier per step is now worth more than squeezing another percentage point out of the planner.

A note for learners: do not benchmark a small model against a frontier model on frontier benchmarks. Benchmark it on the subtask you actually need it for. Ember at Index 36 will fail at graduate physics — it will also finish 400 routing decisions for the cost of one Opus 5.5 call. The skill worth developing is the one that lets you decompose a job into steps and pick the cheapest model that passes each step reliably. That is cheaper to develop than it looks and more valuable than chasing frontier scores.
